newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia annexation of East Timor marked quietly.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia annexation of East Timor marked quietly.

text.p: The 21st anniversary of the Indonesia's annexation of East Timor was marked quietly in the former Portuguese colony on Thursday and Jakarta concedes there is no quick solution to the problems of the troubled territory.

Residents said Dili, the capital of predominantly Catholic East Timor, was quiet as offices and shops closed for a national holiday in mainly-Moslem Indonesia marking the birth of the Prophet Mohammad.
"There is a flag raising ceremony tomorrow morning to mark integration day, but today everything is calm and quiet," one resident said by telephone from Dili.

Indonesia invaded East Timor in December 1975 and declared the territory its 27th province on July 17, 1976, in an act not recognised by the United Nations, which still regards Portugal as the territory's administering power.

There is still armed and political resistance to Jakarta's rule from a small group of armed rebels in the territory's hills and a clandestine political movement in urban areas centred on the Fretilin pro-independence movement.

Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas is involved in talks with his Portuguese counterpart under the umbrella of the U.N. Secretary-General to try to find an acceptable solution to the East Timor question.
However, Alatas warned Indonesian legislators who said they were "bored" with the issue of East Timor to expect no quick fix.

"We don't know when the East Timor issue will be over. The problem of East Timor also depends on Portugal and the United Nations, which make it an issue," Alatas told a parliamentary commission dealing with foreign policy.
"So if Portugal is not ready yet to solve it, the effort to find a solution will go on and on," he said.
Indonesia also has secessionist movements in the eastern-most province of Irian Jaya bordering Papua New Guinea and in Aceh on the tip of Sumatra island on the western end of the archipelago.

The official Antara news agency on Thursday quoted army spokesman Brigadier-General Robik Mukav as saying these movements were the result of frustration with uneven development rather than a desire for self-determination.

"The rebel groups which call themselves Free Aceh, Fretilin and the Free Papua Movement (OPM) are not ABRI's (the armed forces) enemy, but our brothers, Indonesian citizens who feel they have not yet enjoyed the results of development," Mukav said.

Detentions have been reported after an upsurge in violence in East Timor on the eve of Indonesia's May 29 national elections. At least 37 people, including 16 policeman and one soldier in a single ambush, died in the violence.
A number of requests by Jakarta-based foreign journalists for travel documents to visit East Timor since that time have been either unanswered or rejected.
Police have said that more than 70 people have been detained over the same period and international human rights groups have said they fear those in detention are tortured on a regular basis.
Antara quoted East Timor military commander Colonel Slamat Sidabutar on Thursday as denying such charges.
"If there is an anti-integration group overseas who accuses ABRI of violating human rights it needs to be asked, whose human rights?" Sidabutar said.
"Those whose name is "anti" of course do not want to see the actual existing conditions," he said.

Indonesia says the people of East Timor, through a meeting of tribal leaders, freely chose in 1976 to integrate with its huge neighbour and as such there is no need for a referendum on self-determination.
